name: The Impulse and Relativity Mars lander
short_status: Dormant rather than cancelled: announced on 19 July 2022 for a launch as soon as late 2024, moved to 2026 in May 2023, and unmentioned by either company since. No hardware, customer or payload has ever been shown.
page_title: The Impulse and Relativity Mars lander
tagline: Impulse Space and Relativity Space · United States · Lander · 2022 · Announced Planned
stats: announcement date, for a launch as soon as the late 2024 Mars window
the last time either company publicly discussed the mission
customers, payloads, prices or hardware ever made public

facts.label: The announcement
facts.value: 19 July 2022, from El Segundo, California, issued jointly by Impulse Space and Relativity Space and described as the first commercial mission to Mars. The anticipated launch window started in 2024, and Relativity held an exclusive agreement to launch the mission from Cape Canaveral running through 2029.

facts.label: Division of labour
facts.value: Impulse Space would build the Mars Cruise Vehicle, the entry capsule and the lander itself. Relativity Space would launch the stack on Terran R, then described as fully reusable and entirely 3D printed, and later redesigned as partially reusable.

facts.label: The architecture
facts.value: As described by the companies in 2022 and by NextSpaceflight's listing, all in the future tense: a cruise vehicle would carry the encapsulated lander for more than six months, inject the entry capsule onto a landing trajectory and detach; the capsule would use a heatshield and parachute to slow down; the lander would then perform a propulsive landing using purpose-built engines developed in-house at Impulse. None of that hardware has been shown.

facts.label: What the founders said
facts.value: Tom Mueller, Impulse founder and chief executive: "One of the most challenging aspects of landing on Mars is the 'glide stage,' which involves an aeroshell to encapsulate the lander for the survival of Mars entry." Tim Ellis, then Relativity co-founder and chief executive: "With the delivery capabilities of Terran R coupled with Impulse's in-space transportation, we are bringing humanity one step closer to making Mars a reality."

facts.label: What was never disclosed
facts.value: Lander mass, dimensions, payload capacity, payload identity, customers, price and total cost. On cost the companies would say only that it would be "significantly less than previous Mars missions" by building on JPL's work. For scale, SpaceNews noted that InSight, the most recent JPL static lander, cost NASA 814 million dollars including launch but excluding partner instruments.

facts.label: The delay was anticipated
facts.value: The companies planned a 2024 launch but wrote the exclusive agreement to run to 2029. Their own explanation, in a written response to SpaceNews in July 2022: "With launch windows occurring every two years, extending the agreement to 2029 allows for multiple launch options should we need them."

facts.label: The slip
facts.value: Reported by SpaceNews on 24 May 2023 from the Humans to Mars Summit: executives from both companies said the mission was now scheduled for 2026. No reason was given. Relativity had announced in April 2023 that a redesigned Terran R would debut in 2026, two years later than previously planned.

facts.label: The propulsion
facts.value: Impulse announced on 10 May 2023 that it had completed qualification testing of Saiph, a five pounds-force thruster, for its first low Earth orbit mission; Barry Matsumori, then Impulse chief operating officer, said the same thruster would handle the Mars lander's cruise manoeuvres. A larger engine, Rigel, at 180 pounds-force, was to perform the landing.

facts.label: The business plan around it
facts.value: Not one lander but a series. Josh Brost, then senior vice president of revenue operations at Relativity, called it a "constant supply chain to Mars." Matsumori: "We will take advantage of the window every 2.2 years and take at least one mission up," with a catalogue of payload options driving which missions actually flew. The companies hoped NASA would become a customer, in the way it buys lunar deliveries through Commercial Lunar Payload Services.

facts.label: The heritage claimed
facts.value: The companies said in May 2023 that they planned to leverage designs and technologies from NASA's InSight lander, including its heat shield. Brost: "We're not trying to reinvent the wheel," adding that "doing a clean-sheet design of a lander is an insane, monumental engineering feat." This was a stated intention. Nothing was delivered.

facts.label: The silence, first reported
facts.value: SpaceNews, 14 October 2025, in an article about Impulse's new lunar cargo lander: the companies said in 2022 that the first Mars mission could launch as soon as 2024, "but Terran R has yet to make its debut flight, and there have been no recent updates on the Mars lander project."

facts.label: The silence, confirmed
facts.value: SpaceNews, 17 June 2026, reporting Relativity's new Mars orbiter: "Before Schmidt took over Relativity Space, the company pursued a different nongovernmental Mars mission. Relativity and Impulse Space announced in 2022 plans for a Mars lander mission that would launch on Terran R, with the lander itself built by Impulse. The companies said in 2023 they were planning to launch the mission as soon as 2026, but neither has provided recent updates on those plans."

facts.label: What Impulse is doing instead
facts.value: As of 24 August 2026 the company's own site lists three vehicles, Helios, Mira and Rideshare, none of them for Mars, and the flights it advertises run to low Earth orbit, geostationary orbit and, from 2028, the lunar surface. There is no Mars mission and no Mars vehicle on it. The company's public update index, 48 items from March 2022 to 13 August 2026, contains exactly one Mars item: the announcement of 19 July 2022.

facts.label: What Relativity is doing instead
facts.value: Eric Schmidt became chief executive in March 2025. On 17 June 2026 the company announced the Interplanetary Sciences Program, whose first mission is a Mars science and telecommunications orbiter for late 2028 carrying a NASA Ames instrument suite. It is a different spacecraft, a different partner and a different funding model from the Impulse lander.

facts.label: The listings disagree
facts.value: NextSpaceflight, checked on 24 August 2026, lists "Impulse Space's Mars Mission" on Terran R from Launch Complex 16 with a liftoff time of "No Earlier Than 2028." Aggregator sites that mirror older data still carry a launch date of 31 December 2026 with a status of "To Be Determined," which is a year-only placeholder rather than a schedule. On lookingforwardto.com the row's own "last source update" stamp reads 10 August 2024, and its window opens and closes at the same instant, 31 December 2026 00:00 UTC.

facts.label: The rocket
facts.value: Terran R has still never flown. Relativity's July 2026 company update, published 11 August 2026, reports stage one structural qualification complete and the second stage cryoproofed at NASA Stennis, but gives no first flight date. Industry sources told SpaceNews in June 2026 they expected the debut to slip to 2027.

timeline: Impulse Space and Relativity Space announce a commercial Mars lander with an anticipated launch window starting in 2024, and an exclusive launch agreement running through 2029. Neither company has flown a mission of any kind.

SpaceNews reports the announcement, notes that no size, mass, payload capacity, customer or cost was disclosed, and records the companies' own acknowledgement that the 2029 end date on the agreement exists to allow for multiple launch windows should they need them.
Relativity's Terran 1 makes its only flight and fails to reach orbit. The company shelves it to focus on Terran R, the vehicle the Mars mission depends on.
Relativity announces that a redesigned Terran R will debut in 2026, two years later than previously planned. The Mars mission's 2024 window becomes unreachable.

Impulse announces that it has completed qualification testing of Saiph, a five pounds-force thruster, for its first low Earth orbit mission. Impulse says the same thruster will handle the Mars lander's cruise manoeuvres, and that a 180 pounds-force engine called Rigel will do the landing.

SpaceNews reports from the Humans to Mars Summit that executives from both companies now put the mission in 2026, with no reason given for the delay. They describe a series of landers at every window, a payload catalogue, and InSight heat shield heritage. This is the last time either company discusses the mission in public.
Eric Schmidt becomes chief executive of Relativity Space while making a significant investment. Company communications thereafter concentrate on Terran R hardware.

Impulse announces a lunar cargo lander instead, capable of three tonnes to the lunar surface from 2028, built around its Helios transfer vehicle. In the same article SpaceNews records that there have been no recent updates on the Mars lander project.

Impulse announces a 500 million dollar Series D to build in-space mobility infrastructure. Its published mission roadmap covers low Earth orbit, geostationary transfer and lunar delivery. Mars is absent from it.

Relativity announces a NASA-instrumented Mars science orbiter for 2028 under a new Interplanetary Sciences Program. SpaceNews frames the Impulse lander as the different, pre-Schmidt Mars mission on which neither company has provided recent updates.

Checked: Impulse's public vehicle and mission lists contain no Mars element; its update index carries exactly one Mars item, from July 2022. NextSpaceflight lists the mission as no earlier than 2028. Aggregator trackers still show a placeholder of 31 December 2026. Terran R has not flown.
